1360: They marched past my post at exactly the right pace, and my hand saluted before my brain could object.
1361: I asked for their papers. They looked so certain that I found myself apologizing for asking.
1362: They wore a coat with more buttons than a general's, and I stood a little straighter without deciding to.
1363: They walked in like they owned the gate, the wall, and quite possibly me. So I held the door.
1364: My whole job is stopping strangers. This one nodded once, and I stopped only myself.
1365: They demanded the grandest entrance, so I opened both halves of the gate for a single person.
1366: I have turned away important people before. This one I waved through, and I still cannot tell you why.
1367: They inspected my uniform, told me a button was crooked, and I thanked them for the correction.
1368: They strode past carrying something that gleamed, and I assumed anyone that shiny was allowed.
1369: I stood at attention for the visiting dignitary. There was no dignitary. There was only them.
1370: They asked me to hold their heavy bag while they adjusted their hat in my polished boots.
1371: My orders said let no one pass. Their posture said otherwise, and their posture outranked me.
1372: They saluted me first, which no one has ever done, so I saluted back and let them through.
1373: They walked the length of my watch as if reviewing troops, and I found myself hoping I had measured up.
1374: I guard this post day and night. For one glorious minute I guarded it for them instead.
1375: They complimented the shine on my helmet, then borrowed it to check their reflection.
1376: The gate is my responsibility. They opened it themselves, thanked me for my service, and were gone.
1377: They filled out no forms and answered no questions, yet somehow I saluted the whole time.
1378: I have stood this watch for years without moving. They made me step aside with one raised eyebrow.
1379: They wanted a guard of honour, so for thirty seconds I was one, and then I was just confused.
1380: They joined the council uninvited, agreed with every wise thing I said, and I glowed like a fool.
1381: They asked, purely for their studies, exactly how the crown jewels were guarded at night.
1382: They bowed lower than protocol requires, and the whole court decided they must be very important.
1383: They corrected the court historian on a date, and the historian thanked them and changed the record.
1384: They flattered the queen so smoothly that I nearly recommended them for a title of their own.
1385: They sat in my chair at the council table, and I stood, delighted to have given it to them.
1386: They arrived late to every meeting, and the whole council quietly learned to start later.
1387: They complimented each courtier by name, and by supper the whole palace adored a stranger.
1388: They studied the royal portraits closely and asked which jewels in them still existed.
1389: They disagreed with me once, gently, and by evening I had come round to disagreeing with myself.
1390: They wore more gold than the throne and somehow made the throne look underdressed.
1391: They asked me, in confidence, whether the biggest crown was as heavy as it looked.
1392: They advised the king better than I did, and the king noticed, and I did not enjoy it.
1393: They wanted to hold the sceptre to appreciate the craftsmanship, and the court applauded.
1394: They charmed the guards, the cooks, and the treasurer, all before the afternoon tea.
1395: They claimed a title I had never heard of, and no one, myself included, dared to admit it.
1396: They gave advice on a matter well outside their business, and we all wrote it down like law.
1397: They tried on the smaller crowns for scale, and the whole court agreed it suited them.
1398: They praised the palace security at length, then asked one very specific question about it.
1399: They swept into the throne room, and half the councillors forgot which of us they served.
